The Last Light

Elric had kept the Maren Point light for thirty-one years, and in that time the sea had taken his father, his brother, and, in a smaller way, his wife—she'd left when the isolation became unbearable, though he never blamed her for it.

Each evening he climbed the spiral stairs, one hundred and forty-two steps he'd counted so many times the number felt like a heartbeat. He'd wind the mechanism, trim the wick, and watch the beam sweep across water the color of old iron.

Tonight the fog rolled in thick as wool. Somewhere out there, a fishing boat's engine coughed and died. He heard it before he saw it—the particular silence of a vessel adrift.

He lit a second lamp, an old habit passed down from his father, and carried it to the rocks below, waving it in slow arcs. Minutes stretched. Then a voice, hoarse but alive, called back through the mist.

Three men stumbled ashore before dawn, half-frozen but breathing.

Elric fed them broth and said little. He never spoke of the light as duty. It was simpler than that: the sea took what it wanted, but not tonight, not while he still had oil enough to burn.
